summary: Ember is an interactive dashboard designed to show whether a small fire will keep burning in the air planned for Moon and Mars habitats, about 34% oxygen at 8.2 psi. Using real NASA Physical Sciences Informatics data, mainly the CFI-G gas-flame and FLEX fuel-droplet experiments flown on the space station, our tool finds where fires stay lit and where they go out, and labels every answer as tested, estimated or untested. It empowers habitat designers, safety engineers and researchers to quickly check a fire scenario, trace the answer back to the exact NASA tests, and see where the data stops: for example, NASA has no gas-flame test with a result between 25% and 33% oxygen, the planned Moon-base range. In future, the same approach can cover solid materials such as fabrics and plastics, and the results of new tests at Moon and Mars gravity as NASA runs them. Ember addresses a major challenge: most tools give an answer for any input, even far from real data. Yet for crew safety, knowing what has never been tested matters as much as knowing what has. Making those gaps visible is essential for safe habitat design and for planning the next fire experiments.
details:
Ember is a web app that turns NASA’s microgravity fire experiments into answers people can use. The question behind it is simple: if a small fire starts in a Moon or Mars habitat, where the air will have more oxygen than on the space station, will it keep burning? NASA’s data on this is public but spread across many tables in different formats, so we brought it together into one place and built tools around it.


What’s in the app
• Simulation: an interactive flame on fabric or acrylic. You change gravity (space station, Moon, Mars, Earth), oxygen, pressure and airflow, and watch the flame react. It’s there to build intuition. It says clearly that it’s an illustration and tells you when NASA has no tests for the conditions you picked.
• Fire check: the main tool. Describe a gas leak or a fuel drop (fuel, oxygen, pressure, size) and Ember answers in one of three ways:

  1. tested: NASA ran something close, so you see the real result;
  2. estimated: it’s between tests, so you get a chance with a range;
  3. untested: it’s outside NASA’s tests, so no number at all.

It also draws the oxygen line, showing where a fire starts to keep burning, and suggests the next tests that would teach us the most. The full result downloads as a report.
• Fire map: a 3D map of every NASA test with a known ending, placed by oxygen, pressure and fuel and colored by whether the fire kept burning or went out. The Moon and Mars base air is marked, so you can see right away where NASA hasn’t tested.
• Find data: search all the NASA tables, reports and papers in one place, see each source’s credibility, and export the results as CSV, JSON or BibTeX. You can also ask a question in plain words, and the AI must cite a NASA source for every sentence or that sentence is removed.
• Statistics: an overview of the data and the models: how many tests there are, how the models scored against a simple baseline, and the path from NASA’s raw tables to the final answers.
• Research paper: a short paper on our method and findings, built from the same code as the app.


Benefits and impact

  • Honest answers: Ember never guesses outside the data. Every result is labelled tested, estimated or untested, so users know exactly how much to trust it.
  • Traceable: every answer links to the exact NASA test rows behind it, and NASA’s data is never changed. Clear errors are removed with a reason, and doubtful values are only flagged.
  • Fair models: we compared several models on NASA test campaigns they had never seen. A model is used only if it beats a simple guess.
  • Gaps become a plan: Ember doesn’t hide missing data. It shows it, and suggests which experiments should be run next.
  • Useful for real people: habitat designers and safety teams can check a scenario in seconds, and researchers can see where more experiments are needed. The same question matters on Earth, in hospitals and anywhere else with oxygen-rich air.

How we built it

  • Data: a Python script downloads 19 tables from NASA’s PSI and checks each file with a checksum. We mapped all the tables into one format, stored them as Parquet files, and query them with DuckDB.
  • Cleaning: clear errors (duplicates, impossible values) are removed with a reason; anything doubtful is flagged but never changed.
  • Models: with scikit-learn we compared logistic regression, a random forest and a Gaussian process on oxygen, pressure, size and fuel. Each model was tested on NASA test campaigns it had never seen and had to beat a simple baseline. The Gaussian process won, and it also shows how unsure it is.
  • Answers: each request is compared with real NASA tests to decide whether it’s tested, estimated or untested. The oxygen line and the next-test suggestions come from the same models.
  • AI: search uses BM25 keyword matching. The Ask feature sends NASA passages to an AI model on Groq, and our code deletes any sentence without a valid NASA citation.
  • App: a Python and FastAPI backend, and a React and TypeScript frontend. It’s tested with pytest and Playwright, packaged with Docker, and hosted on Modal.
  • AI use: Claude (Anthropic), through Claude Code, helped write the code. The ideas and decisions were ours.
